help.content:
[font_size=26][b]What is GAN Organism Arena?[/b][/font_size]

GAN Organism Arena is an artificial-life aquarium. This rewrite moves the actual simulation from a 2D cellular field into a real three-dimensional world. Organisms have true X/Y/Z positions, swim in all directions, seek resources, avoid threats, reproduce with mutation, develop bodies in three dimensions and accumulate progressively richer cognitive/communication states.

[b]The idea behind it[/b]
The original project was inspired by Conway's Game of Life: a famous cellular automaton in which simple local rules can create surprisingly complex patterns. This version keeps that fascination with emergence, but it does not try to force classic Conway rules into 3D. Instead it treats each lifeform as an evolving developmental program. A genome controls tendencies such as symmetry, elongation, limb growth, fins, armor, sensors, neural development, curiosity, cooperation, aggression, metabolism and vocal behavior.

[b]Open-ended development[/b]
There is deliberately no semantic final body stage such as 'human' or 'maximum creature'. Complexity and cognition can continue increasing. Rendering uses a practical visible-cell budget so performance remains bounded, while body proportions, appendage lengths, branching, sensors, neural density and communication can continue changing. This means the simulation can remain computationally finite without declaring evolution finished.

[b]3D body development[/b]
Bodies are constructed from instanced low-poly biological cells in local 3D space. Early lifeforms may look colony-like. With development they can gain an axial body, spine-like support, neural chains, heads, paired extremities, hands/feet, fin fans, armor plates, feather-like structures and long sensor appendages. The exact direction depends on the genome rather than a fixed ladder.

[b]Cognition and language[/b]
Every organism has internal energy, hunger, fear, curiosity, social tendency, experience and episodic memory. Its language stage emerges from neural development, sensory drive, vocal drive, lineage and complexity. Communication intentionally progresses from elemental sounds to syllables, symbolic tokens, phrases, sentences and increasingly compositional thoughts. Windows TTS can vocalize the translated thought stream; the internal lifeform itself is still represented as an evolving artificial signaling system.

[b]Movement / observation[/b]
Mouse: look around.
W/S: swim forward/back.
A/D: strafe left/right.
Q/E: descend/ascend.
Shift: fast swim.
Mouse wheel: optical zoom in/out. Shift + mouse wheel: change observer speed.
Escape: release/capture mouse.
Left mouse: select organism under the crosshair.
Right mouse: follow/unfollow selected organism.
Tab: select next organism.

[b]Main hotkeys[/b]
F10: Settings. Simulation pauses while Settings is open.
F1: This help. Simulation pauses while Help is open.
Space: manual pause/resume.
G: inject a new random genome into the aquarium.
1: Natural body view.
2: Cell/tissue view.
3: Neural view.
4: Energy view.
F8: export selected organism as an OBJ snapshot.
F12: save screenshot.

[b]Scientific views[/b]
Natural: body-family coloration with sensors/fins/armor differentiated subtly.
Cell: highlights tissue roles such as skeleton-like support, neural cells, sensors and fins.
Neural: dims most tissue and emphasizes neural/sensory structures.
Energy: colors the entire organism according to its current energy.

[b]Settings explained[/b]
Language: loads editable JSON translation files from language/. English is the fallback.
Rendering backend: Forward+ (Vulkan, best visual quality on modern GPUs), Mobile (lighter Vulkan path), or Compatibility (OpenGL, widest fallback). A restart is required because Godot chooses the renderer before the project starts.
Fullscreen: switches the window mode immediately.
Scientific view mode: same as keys 1-4.
Directional light / sun: fixed directional presets or an automatic slowly moving sun.
Simulation speed multiplier: changes world-time speed without tying it to rendering FPS.
3D simulation ticks per second: how often organisms make behavioral/evolutionary decisions. Lower values save CPU while rendering can remain smooth.
Evolution rate: multiplies physical/cognitive development speed.
Maximum living organisms: population safety cap.
3D nutrient particle count: density of edible energy particles in the volume.
Maximum visible body cells per organism: primary GPU/CPU visual complexity budget. This is not an evolution cap; it is only an LOD budget.
Body morphology refresh interval: how often a changed developmental state is rebuilt into visible body cells. Higher values substantially reduce CPU overhead in long runs.
Thought output: Off, text, Windows TTS, or both.
Thought interval: minimum time between rotating organism thought outputs.
Per-organism episodic memory events: bounded event memory; older events are discarded so long simulations do not grow without limit.
Rebuild organism bodies / shader resources: regenerates visible body instances and re-applies lighting/material resources after graphical changes.

[b]Performance architecture[/b]
Behavior/evolution runs at a configurable low tick rate while camera/rendering remains frame-rate driven. Organism bodies use MultiMesh GPU instancing and move as whole Node3D objects; their hundreds of local body cells are not individually re-transformed every frame. Body geometry is rebuilt only when developmental complexity crosses a visible threshold or the refresh interval expires. History is bounded to explicit events instead of recording every evolution step.

[b]OBJ export[/b]
F8 exports the currently selected organism into exports/obj/. The current prototype exports each biological body cell as a compact octahedral polygon component, preserving the evolved 3D silhouette for Blender and other 3D software.

[b]Files[/b]
settings/config.json - persistent options.
language/*.json - editable translations.
logs/latest_runtime.log - current runtime diagnostics.
exports/obj/ - organism mesh exports.
screenshots/ - F12 captures.

[b]License[/b]
GAN Organism Arena is provided under the MIT License. See LICENSE.txt.

[b]Morphological evolution in alpha7[/b]
Seven topology families seed the morphology space: serpentine, fusiform, radial, ray, branching, crustacean-like and cephalopod-like. These are not fixed species. Continuous proportion genes, ordinary mutations, rare macro-mutations and sexual crossover can push descendants far from their parents. Genomes also have a developmental viability score: excessively costly, unsupported combinations lose energy quickly and may disappear instead of reproducing. Social steering now has a preferred separation distance to prevent organisms from locking into permanent oscillating contact. RMB follow uses anatomical rear/focus anchors, so the observer stays behind the tail/rear rather than chasing the organism centre.

[b]Evolving habitats — alpha8[/b]
Keys 5-9 switch the ecological stage. 5 is fully aquatic. 6 adds seabed/islands. 7 creates a coast with meaningful land. 8 emphasizes land, shallows and air. 9 keeps water, land and open sky together. Every higher habitat stage expands X/Y/Z world size by one configured unit; NumPad + and - expand/shrink it manually. Aquatic, terrestrial and flight adaptation are heritable genes, so changing habitat creates selection pressure instead of teleporting every species into instant competence.

[b]Ecology and social evolution[/b]
Organisms can court nearby viable partners, form loose family/pack groups, establish simple rank spacing and evolve predator-like pursuit. Cross-family and cross-body-plan mating is intentionally more permissive than alpha7. At population capacity, natural deaths open places for offspring; no automatic complexity-based culling occurs.

[b]Sound ecosystem[/b]
Procedural ambient sound changes with habitat. Organism calls are spatial 3D sounds; family and language stage alter pitch, syllable count and harmonic complexity. This channel is independent from Windows TTS, which remains a translated thought output. Audio can be disabled or tuned in Settings.

[b]Ecology — alpha10[/b]
The world defaults to 144 × 86.4 × 144 units: twice every previous dimension. Shorelines, terrain height, food and movement share one surface. Keys 5–9 change habitat; only 8/9 provide open sky for powered flight.
Gill, lung and skin respiration determine oxygen reserves. Amphibious organisms can revisit water and land; dry skin and limited breath force unsuitable specialists to retreat. Powerful swimming costs energy and stamina. Flight requires adequate wings, support, low loading, air respiration, practice and open sky.
Heritable combinations can yield pack pursuit/flanking, ambush interception, camouflage/hiding, cleaning, parasitism, tool manipulation, upright gait, small insect-like bodies, rooted filters, photosynthetic growth and land trees. Tools are collected at rocky food patches, open finite food stocks and wear out. Learned hunting/tool/flight skills develop during a lifetime; offspring inherit predispositions, not those memories.
These are bounded artificial-life rules, not a biological prediction or a general intelligence. Forms need not match Earth species, but evolution operates inside the implemented gene and body grammar.
There is no automatic replacement of extinct populations by default. G injects a new random organism; Auto reseed in Settings restores the optional rescue behavior. The population cap is a performance limit; natural mortality opens space. Neither intelligence nor body complexity receives a forced survival bonus.

[b]Body coverings — alpha12[/b]
Skin thickness, scales, feathers, fur/bristles, mucus, membranes, horns/spines, beaks and pigment patterns are inherited, mutate and can be combined. Feathers have visible vanes and quills; they can grow without fins or flight. Flight still requires suitable wings, body structure, breathing, practice and open sky.
Thick skin and scales reduce drying and bite damage but restrict skin breathing. Fur and feathers insulate against cold; in warm areas they can retain too much heat and under water increase drag. Mucus reduces drying and some drag. Horns add protection and load; beaks improve bites. Body coverings cost energy. The temperature gradient and these effects are simplified simulation rules.
Surfaces use stylized 3D cells within the existing visual budget; they are not photographic materials. The inspector lists coverings separately and shows local temperature.
